word_bank.example: Saying 'life is a journey' is a common metaphor in English literature.
The protagonist of the novel is a young woman searching for her missing brother.
The dark clouds described in chapter one were foreshadowing the tragedy ahead.
The novel shifts between two different narratives — one in the past and one in the present.
The broken clock in the story is symbolism for the character's refusal to move forward.
He mostly reads in the crime genre but recently tried science fiction.
The central theme of the book is the conflict between loyalty and personal freedom.
The climax of the novel comes when the two brothers finally confront each other.
The epilogue revealed what happened to each character ten years later.
Many readers interpret the story as an allegory for political oppression.

stage_2_story.text_en: Every Thursday evening, a small group gathered around the table in Miriam's living room for the book club. This month, they had read a short but dense novel — a story about a painter who returns to his hometown after thirty years to settle his father's affairs. The protagonist arrives cold and detached, certain he will leave within a week. He does not. Miriam opened the discussion by asking whether anyone had noticed the foreshadowing in the very first paragraph — the painter stares at a cracked window that he does not bother to fix. 'That crack tells you everything,' she said. 'He is a man who leaves things broken.' Yaron pushed back gently. He argued that the cracked window was more than foreshadowing — it was symbolism, a recurring image that appeared each time the protagonist avoided a difficult truth. The others agreed. Someone brought up the central theme: that we inherit not just property from our parents, but also their unresolved pain. The novel was also, the group decided, an allegory for a whole generation of men who had been taught to suppress emotion. But the narrative itself was what most impressed them — non-linear, jumping between decades without confusion, building quietly toward a climax that arrived not with a dramatic confrontation but with a simple letter found in a drawer. The author had written a brief epilogue showing the painter three years later: the house repaired, a new canvas on the wall. Dina, who normally preferred the crime genre, admitted she had cried at the end. She compared the ending to a metaphor — like a seed planted in winter that only blooms the following spring. They stayed around the table for two hours, talking long after the tea had gone cold.
